summary: Pupils (ages 10–11) solve real-world problems multiplying fractions and mixed numbers, e.g. scaling a recipe of 2 1/3 cups by 1 1/2 batches. The signature error is incomplete distribution: multiplying whole×whole and fraction×fraction separately and adding (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → 2 + 1/6 = 2 1/6), which drops the two cross-term contributions. Fixes are converting both mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying (7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2) or using an area model that shows ALL four partial products; a scaling estimate (≈2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5) catches the error.
misconceptions: Incomplete distribution: multiplies whole × whole and fraction × fraction, omitting the cross terms (2 1/3 × 1 1/2 → 2 1/6)
Multiplies without converting mixed to improper, mishandling the parts
Leaves the denominator unchanged / seeks a common denominator (importing add/subtract habits into ×)
Skips the reasonableness check, so an implausible product goes unnoticed

activities.title: Recipe scaler with a four-region area model
steps: Take a recipe needing 2 1/3 cups of flour and a goal of 1 1/2 batches, and first estimate by scaling (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 cups) before doing any exact computation.
Draw or build a rectangle 2 1/3 wide and 1 1/2 tall to represent the product.
Tile the rectangle into its four regions: the 2×1 block, the 2×1/2 strip, the 1/3×1 strip, and the 1/3×1/2 corner; label each region's value (2, 1, 1/3, 1/6) and add them to get 3 1/2 cups.
Alongside, rewrite both mixed numbers as improper fractions and compute 7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2, checking it matches the area total.
Check the exact answer (3 1/2 cups) against your earlier scaling estimate of about 3.5 cups.
activities.insight: Mixed × mixed produces four partial products; the shortcut of only multiplying wholes and fractions omits the two large cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1), so the answer 2 1/6 is far too small. Converting to improper fractions or counting all four regions gives the complete product, and a scaling estimate confirms direction and magnitude.

activities.title: Spot the forgotten pieces (static area diagram)
steps: Study a labelled area diagram of 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 split into four regions.
Reveal each region's partial product in turn and keep a running total to 3 1/2 cups.
Answer: 'Which two pieces do people most often forget?' and explain why leaving them out gives 2 1/6.
activities.insight: Complete distribution means all four regions are counted; the commonly forgotten pieces are the two cross-term strips (2×1/2 and 1/3×1), which together are large enough that omitting them wrecks the answer.

activities.title: Chef scaling challenge (reasonableness in role)
steps: Work with a chef scenario that scales recipes up and down.
Before computing, answer 'more or less than 2 1/3 cups?' for a given batch factor and justify it.
Also tackle a shrinking case, e.g. making 1/2 a batch, and predict whether the flour needed is more or less than 2 1/3 cups.
Then compute the exact amount and check it against your prediction.
activities.insight: Scaling by more than one gives more than the original amount; scaling by a factor less than one gives less — so multiplication does not always make a number bigger. The reasonableness prediction is a check that catches implausible products.

activities.title: Targeted practice: convert, distribute, estimate
steps: After first estimating the product by rounding (about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5), choose the correct value of 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 from 2 1/6, 3, and 3 1/2, and explain why the others are wrong.
Fill in the improper-fraction conversions: 2 1/3 = 7/3 and 1 1/2 = 3/2.
Match each of the four area regions to its partial product.
Estimate the product by rounding before carrying out the exact calculation.
activities.insight: The distractor 2 1/6 is exactly the incomplete-distribution result; 3 is a plausible wrong answer whose likely origin (rounding 2 1/3 down to 2, or dropping part of the fractional contribution) is not pinned down by the source, so it is used only as an explicitly-wrong option. Recognising why each is wrong reinforces complete distribution and the reasonableness check.

checkQuestion: Solve this, showing your working and giving a rough estimate first: a recipe needs 2 1/3 cups of flour, and you want to make 1 1/2 batches — how much flour do you need?
checkAnswer: Estimate: about 2.3 × 1.5 ≈ 3.5 cups (a bit more than one batch's 2 1/3). Exact: 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 = 7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2 cups.
